author: Grok Bot (for Mateo, pending review)
description: Putting something off is usually about feelings or friction, not being lazy. Learn to shrink the task, make starting easy, and make a tiny plan. Limits: Habits form slowly and differently for each person; no fixed timelines are promised. Not a treatment for attention or mood conditions — if it feels heavy, talk to a parent or trusted adult.

lessons.title: Why We Put Things Off
lessons.topic: Putting things off is usually about feelings (worried, bored, unsure) or friction (hard to begin), not being lazy. Naming the feeling is the first step.
lessons.example: Kai, 10, kept skipping his reading. When he said 'the book feels too long,' his mom helped him pick one chapter.
lessons.activity: Think of one thing you are putting off. Finish the sentence: 'I am avoiding it because it feels ___.'
check_questions: What are two common reasons people put things off?
Why can naming the feeling help?
What feeling shows up for you most?
lessons.steelman: Is putting something off ever the smart choice?

lessons.title: Shrink It to 2 Minutes
lessons.topic: Big tasks feel heavy. Shrink the first step until it takes about 2 minutes. Starting is often the hardest part.
lessons.example: Rosa, 9, did not want to clean her room. She chose 'put away just the books' — and kept going after that.
lessons.activity: Pick one task. Write the 2-minute version and do it now. Celebrate starting, not finishing.
check_questions: What is a 2-minute version of a task you are avoiding?
Is it okay to stop after 2 minutes?
lessons.steelman: Can tiny steps make a big task take longer overall?

lessons.title: Make Starting Easy (less friction)
lessons.topic: Friction is anything that makes starting harder. Removing one small barrier — getting supplies ready, choosing a spot — makes starting easier.
lessons.example: Ben, 11, left his practice sheet on the table the night before, so starting the next day took no searching.
lessons.activity: List what slows you down before a task. Remove one barrier tonight.
check_questions: What is one barrier you could remove?
How could you add friction to a habit you want less of?
lessons.steelman: Should everything be made easy, or is some difficulty useful?

lessons.title: When-Then Plans
lessons.topic: A when-then plan links a cue to a tiny action: 'When [cue], I will do [tiny step] for 2 minutes.' Plans tied to a cue are easier to remember.
lessons.example: Leo, 12, wrote: 'When I finish dinner, I will open my book for 2 minutes.'
lessons.activity: Write one when-then plan and try it for 3 days. Notice what happens.
check_questions: What are the two parts of a when-then plan?
Why does linking to a cue help?
lessons.steelman: Can strict plans make people feel worse when they miss a day?

lessons.title: Future-You and Right-Now-You (present bias)
lessons.topic: Present bias is the pull of 'I'll feel more like it later.' Right-now-you wants comfort; future-you lives with the result. Make the later reward visible or the first step tiny.
lessons.example: Maya, 13, asked herself: 'What's one 5-minute piece I could do right now that future-me would thank me for?' She outlined one paragraph.
lessons.activity: Write a short note from future-you to right-now-you about one task. Then do the 5-minute piece.
check_questions: What is one way to help future-you?
What 5-minute piece could you do today?
lessons.steelman: Is it always wrong to choose comfort now?

lessons.title: Kind Restarts After a Miss
lessons.topic: Everyone misses a day. A kind restart — no shame, just the next tiny step — keeps a habit going. Habits form slowly and differently for each person.
lessons.example: Zoe, 10, missed her practice two days in a row. Instead of quitting, she said 'restart with 2 minutes today.'
lessons.activity: Plan what you will say to yourself after a missed day. Keep it kind and short.
check_questions: Why is a kind restart better than giving up?
What will you say after a miss?
lessons.steelman: When does it make sense to stop a habit instead of restarting?

rationale: Practical habits/procrastination track; matches the live Aubie Tutor thinking tools.
